question: No maximum catch quotas have been set for squid within the EU, which is not the case for many other target species. As catches of traditional target species such as plaice and sole are declining, Dutch fishing vessels in the North Sea and surrounding waters are increasingly turning to squid. As a result, fishing pressure on this unregulated species has increased significantly.1 In the 2023–2024 season, more than 3.
6 million squid were caught by Dutch cutters2. Scientists warn that the rapidly growing industry of squid fishing could put the species at risk3. 1.

Given their intrinsic value and their role as a food source for dolphins, whales, seals, larger fish species and seabirds, amongst others, to what extent does the Commission consider it important to protect squid from overfishing?

What is the Commission’s assessment of the significantly increased fishing pressure on unregulated species such as squid, red gurnard and mullet, and the warning that these species will become endangered unless maximum catch limits are set in the near future?

The Common Fisheries Policy dictates that the EU must apply the precautionary principle when regulating fisheries. To what extent is the absence of maximum catch limits for heavily fished species consistent with the precautionary principle, and what measures will the Commission take in the short term to prevent squid populations and other unregulated species from becoming endangered?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) Non-quota stocks (NQS) play a key ecological and socio-economic role, particularly for coastal communities. The Commission is committed to ensuring their sustainable exploitation in line with the objectives of the Common Fisheries Policy.

The Commission acknowledges concerns regarding increasing fishing pressure on certain NQS, like squid, and works to improve both scientific knowledge and management of these stocks, like those shared with the UK. For NQS, some conservation and management measures may be applied, depending on the fishery and the available scientific evidence.

Catch limits are thus not the only tool available under a precautionary approach. At EU level, squid fisheries are currently managed mainly through technical measures, complemented where appropriate by national measures.

In addition, the EU and the UK are cooperating on the management of shared NQS, like scientific exchanges on species such as cuttlefish, whelks and octopus, as well as ongoing work on Channel king scallops and brown crab. The marine strategy framework directive1 requires Member States to achieve good environmental status for their marine waters.

In doing so, as part of their marine strategies, they must set and comply with threshold values at species level for various species groups, like cephalopods2. These thresholds must ensure that ‘the population abundance of the species is not adversely affected due to anthropogenic pressures, such that its long-term viability is ensured’ and that ‘the population demographic characteristics (e.g.
body size or age class structure, sex ratio, fecundity, and survival rates) of the species are indicative of a healthy population which is not adversely affected due to anthropogenic pressure’.
